nodes.label: Flowchart diagrams skill
nodes.rationale: Exists because the default failure is not an ugly diagram but one that looks like a flowchart while having no grammar underneath — everything a rectangle, unlabelled branch arrows, explanations stuffed into nodes, and real decisions hidden in sticky notes. A flowchart is a small formal language whose whole point is that a reader can trace a path with a finger without reading every word.

nodes.label: Check it is actually a flowchart
nodes.rationale: Forcing the wrong content into a flowchart is a bigger failure than bad shapes. Comparisons want a table, before/after wants two panels, 'what talks to what' wants an architecture diagram with no start node, and a glossary belongs on its own page — sitting beside a flow it steals attention and is the commonest way a good flow gets buried.

nodes.label: Write the node list before touching XML
nodes.rationale: One line per node tagged with shape and actor, because this catches structural problems while they are still cheap to fix. Two tests fall out of it: any node whose text needs the word 'and' is two nodes, and any node with more than one outgoing arrow is a missing decision.

nodes.label: Hunt the branches the prose forgot
nodes.rationale: Prose describes the happy path; exposing the gaps is most of a diagram's value. Walk the list explicitly: cancel or dismiss, permission gate, validation failure, empty or zero case, failure of the write itself, and already-in-that-state. Anything found that the source material did not mention goes to the user as a question, never into the diagram as an invention.

nodes.label: Shape grammar (six shapes, no more)
nodes.rationale: Stadium for start and end, rectangle for a system step, diamond for a question, parallelogram for what a person sees or answers, cylinder for a table, sticky note for why rather than what. Consistency is what makes shapes readable; a seventh shape invented for one node teaches the reader nothing. Node text works best at twelve words or fewer, asides belong in notes on dashed connectors, and a legend near the title makes the grammar self-teaching.

nodes.label: Every decision exit carries a label
nodes.rationale: An unlabelled branch forces the reader to infer the condition from the destination box, which defeats the diamond. Exits must be mutually exclusive and cover every case, and the diamond holds the question while the answer sits on the arrow.

nodes.label: One cylinder = one table, one operation, one point in the flow
nodes.rationale: 'writes' is not an operation — the reader cannot tell an insert from an update, which is usually the whole point of the step, and reads escape this only because a read has one meaning. The shape is a noun (the table name) and the arrow is a verb (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/UPSERT), kept bare because row counts crowd the busiest part of the canvas and go stale. Never two tables in one cylinder, never a read and a write on one, and the same table touched twice is two cylinders — collapsing them hides the gap where the interesting behaviour lives.

nodes.label: Swimlanes for actor boundaries
nodes.rationale: Use them when steps cross a boundary the reader needs to see, such as browser/server/database, because lanes make visible a fact prose inside boxes cannot show — for example that a flow crosses to the server twice, once to read and once to write. Skip them when everything happens in one place, where they only cost width.

nodes.label: check_flowchart.py validator
nodes.rationale: Reports unlabelled decision exits, processes that branch without a decision, orphaned and dead-end nodes, prose crammed into nodes, overlapping geometry, broken edge references, and pages dominated by one shape type. It is a linter, not a judge: a deliberate second terminator is fine, a silently unlabelled branch is not. Then read one path end to end as a stranger would.

nodes.label: Mermaid as the alternative output
nodes.rationale: Better when the diagram belongs in a README, a code comment or a chat reply — the same grammar with less ceremony, and only the geometry work disappears. Reach for drawio when the user needs to edit it by hand or the diagram is large enough that manual layout beats auto-layout.
